proposalname: Back Country Trails Squak Mountain Crystal Creek Bridge Replacement
proposaldescription: The BCT SM Crystal Creek Bridge (Project) proposes to remove an existing, deteriorated log bridge and replace it with a weathering steel bridge. The existing bridge to be removed is a single log with bolted-on wood (untreated) railings and is thirty-eight (38) feet long. The existing bridge is beyond its serviceable lifespan and must be decommissioned. The proposed bridge will be weathering steel with steel railings and will be eight (80) feet long. The proposed bridge will have light grey Fiber Reinforced Plastic (FRP) decking and concrete abutments. The proposed bridge and abutments will be prefabricated and air-lifted to the site from a nearby staging area. The decking and other incidental materials will be brought to the site by vehicle using the existing trail network. Construction activities will include land clearing, tree removal, and earthwork excavation for installation of the new bridge and abutments. The old bridge and railing will be deposited in the adjacent forest and allowed to decompose naturally. The footing on the south side of the old bridge is constructed of soil-filled bags that were originally filled using soil from the site—after installation of the new bridge, these bags will be emptied in the surrounding forest, and the bags will be removed from the site. The northern footing of the existing bridge rests on native soil. The project will result in impacts to wetland/stream buffers from land clearing and grading for the bridge footings which will be offset by onsite habitat enhancement in the form of removal of man-made structures (soil bag abutments) from the stream bank and decommissioning of portions of the trail leading to the existing bridge that will no longer be needed due to the increase in length of the new bridge. These areas will be planted with native vegetation appropriate for the site conditions.

proposalname: Sammamish River and Waynita Creek Restoration
proposaldescription: The City of Bothell Sammamish River and Waynita Creek Restoration Project aims to restore approximately 12 acres of aquatic and riparian habitat along the Sammamish River and its tributary, Waynita Creek, in King County, Washington. The Sammamish River is impaired by high in-stream temperatures and low dissolved oxygen during summer months. The mainstem Sammamish River also lacks habitat complexity, floodplain connection, and cold-water refuge for salmonids, which increases the importance of habitat along its tributaries. Waynita Creek, a tributary to the Sammamish River, lacks forested riparian habitat, which adversely affects salmon during rearing and spawning by limiting key ecological functions including shading for stream temperature regulation and cover from predators, organic inputs to support prey macroinvertebrate communities, and woody material recruitment for in-stream habitat. The proposed Project addresses these deficiencies through targeted riparian and instream habitat restoration. The overall goal of this Project is to improve juvenile rearing and migration habitat for Chinook and other salmonids, while also creating cold-water refuge areas to support adult salmon during migration through the Sammamish River. This work will provide longterm ecological benefits to salmon and other aquatic and terrestrial species. Since acquiring the property, the City has conducted field studies, evaluated restoration alternatives, and engaged with community stakeholders.

proposalname: Lakewood Marina Eurasian Watermilfoil Control Project
proposaldescription:
Manatee Aquatic LLC is applying for the Aquatic Pesticide and Algae Management General Water Quality Permit (APAM) from the Department of Ecology. 

Manatee Aquatic, LLC proposes selective herbicide treatment of approximately 2 acres of Eurasian watermilfoil (Myriophyllum spicatum), a Class B noxious weed listed under chapter 16-750 WAC, in Lake Washington adjacent to Lakewood Marina (4500 Lake Washington Boulevard S, Seattle, WA 98118).

The product to be applied is Renovate OTF (granular formulation), an EPA-registered aquatic herbicide manufactured by SePRO Corporation containing 8.1% triclopyr triethylamine as the active ingredient. Triclopyr TEA is a selective systemic herbicide that targets dicotyledonous plants while sparing native monocots (pondweeds, grass-like vegetation), making it well-suited for milfoil control in waterbodies where native plant preservation is a co-objective. Application rate: approximately 480 pounds of Renovate OTF per acre, for a total of approximately 960 pounds of product across the 2-acre treatment polygon. Target water column concentration: approximately 1.2–1.8 mg/L triclopyr acid equivalent (below the maximum label concentration of 2.5 mg/L), based on average water depth of 8–12 feet in the treatment area. Application will be by direct broadcast from a flatbed pontoon workboat with a 150 hp outboard motor, performed by a Washington State-licensed commercial pesticide applicator with an aquatic endorsement. A single application is planned for mid-to-late June 2026, with annual maintenance treatments anticipated thereafter.

The project’s purpose is to reduce milfoil density within the marina cove to restore navigability for moored vessels, protect native aquatic habitat from displacement by invasive species, and support continued use of the public Lake Washington Boulevard Trail and adjacent City of Seattle Parks shoreline.

proposalname: Lakewood Marina Eurasian Watermilfoil Control Project
proposaldescription:
Manatee Aquatic LLC is applying for the Aquatic Pesticide and Algae Management General Water Quality Permit (APAM) from the Department of Ecology. 

Manatee Aquatic, LLC proposes selective herbicide treatment of approximately 2 acres of Eurasian watermilfoil (Myriophyllum spicatum), a Class B noxious weed listed under chapter 16-750 WAC, in Lake Washington adjacent to Lakewood Marina (4500 Lake Washington Boulevard S, Seattle, WA 98118).

The product to be applied is Renovate OTF (granular formulation), an EPA-registered aquatic herbicide manufactured by SePRO Corporation containing 8.1% triclopyr triethylamine as the active ingredient. Triclopyr TEA is a selective systemic herbicide that targets dicotyledonous plants while sparing native monocots (pondweeds, grass-like vegetation), making it well-suited for milfoil control in waterbodies where native plant preservation is a co-objective. Application rate: approximately 480 pounds of Renovate OTF per acre, for a total of approximately 960 pounds of product across the 2-acre treatment polygon. Target water column concentration: approximately 1.2–1.8 mg/L triclopyr acid equivalent (below the maximum label concentration of 2.5 mg/L), based on average water depth of 8–12 feet in the treatment area. Application will be by direct broadcast from a flatbed pontoon workboat with a 150 hp outboard motor, performed by a Washington State-licensed commercial pesticide applicator with an aquatic endorsement. A single application is planned for mid-to-late June 2026, with annual maintenance treatments anticipated thereafter.

The project’s purpose is to reduce milfoil density within the marina cove to restore navigability for moored vessels, protect native aquatic habitat from displacement by invasive species, and support continued use of the public Lake Washington Boulevard Trail and adjacent City of Seattle Parks shoreline.

proposaldescription:
King County is issuing a SEPA Environmental Checklist Addendum to supplement the original Environmental Checklist from 2024. In response to comments received on the original SEPA notice, King County modified some elements of the project and is now issuing an Addendum to the Environmental Checklist to reflect those changes. The updated information does not substantially affect the analysis of impacts or the original Determination of Non-Significance, and King County has determined that a new threshold determination is not warranted. An updated project description is provided below.

Island Center Forest is a Forest Stewardship Council® (FSC-C008225) certified working forest demonstrating environmentally sound forest management to protect and restore ecological systems while providing recreational opportunities. King County Department of Natural Resources and Parks (DNRP) has a 30-Year Forest Plan that focuses on climate resilient forests. Long-lived conifer species are typically more climate resilient, but overcrowded, even-aged stands like at Island Center Forest suffer from water and light competition, making them more susceptible to disease and drought. Hotter, drier summers will become common with climate change and exacerbate this problem. The red alder-dominated stands are already suffering from age-related mortality.

DNRP is proposing 45.04 acres of commercial tree harvesting in Island Center Forest across 
eight units, plus 1.1 acres of risk tree felling, and 4.7 acres of drop-and-leave cutting in four 
alder “gap” cuts. The commercial units include: Unit A with 12.9 acres, Unit B includes two 
sub-units (B1 West and B1 Central) that combined total 7.6 acres, Unit C is 7.7 acres, 
Cemetery Unit is 7.7 acres (slightly reduced from original size to avoid trail impacts), 
and a series of three “E” units that cover 9.1 acres total. A new 1.1-acre Risk Tree unit was 
added since the original SEPA for felling and leaving on-site trees that pose a risk to trail 
users.  

The objectives for the Douglas-fir treatments are to shift from overly dense stands to less-dense, 
more diverse and drought-resistant conifer stands; prevent density-dependent tree mortality; slow the spread of laminated root rot and plant with rot-resistant species. In the red alder stands, 
treatments will transition the forest from declining alders to more diverse, climate resilient mixed 
species stands. The treatments will generate timber revenue to support forest stewardship in line 
with the property’s working forest designation, defined in King County’s Comprehensive Plan 
(2022).

The Project includes a retrofit of approximately five blocks of City ROW. The sites included in the 90 Percent Design manage runoff for up to 9.3 acres of effective impervious area. The Project proposes conveyance improvements and installation of bioretention facilities to capture and treat stormwater runoff prior to discharging into Thornton Creek, a tributary of Lake Washington. The Project includes two sites:

1.	Olympic Hills site - This site ultimately discharges stormwater runoff to Littlebrook Creek, a tributary to North Branch Thornton Creek. Treated stormwater runoff will be infiltrated via bioretention facilities. Overflow from the bioretention facilities on 25th Ave NE and NE 127th St is directed to the existing ditch and culvert system along NE 127th St and overflow from the facility on 27th Ave NE connects to the existing on-block public storm drain (PSD). Overflows combine near the intersection of NE 125th St and 28th Ave NE and will continue east along NE 125th St towards Littlebrook Creek.

Island Center Forest is a Forest Stewardship Council® (FSC-C008225) certified working forest demonstrating environmentally sound forest management to protect and restore ecological systems while providing recreational opportunities. King County Department of Natural Resources and Parks (DNRP) has a 30-Year Forest Plan that focuses on climate resilient forests. Long-lived conifer species are typically more climate resilient, but overcrowded, even-aged stands like at Island Center Forest suffer from water and light competition, making them more susceptible to disease and drought. Hotter, drier summers will become common with climate change and exacerbate this problem. The red alder-dominated stands are already suffering from age-related mortality.

DNRP is proposing 45.04 acres of commercial tree harvesting in Island Center Forest across 
eight units, plus 1.1 acres of risk tree felling, and 4.7 acres of drop-and-leave cutting in four 
alder “gap” cuts. The commercial units include: Unit A with 12.9 acres, Unit B includes two 
sub-units (B1 West and B1 Central) that combined total 7.6 acres, Unit C is 7.7 acres, 
Cemetery Unit is 7.7 acres (slightly reduced from original size to avoid trail impacts), 
and a series of three “E” units that cover 9.1 acres total. A new 1.1-acre Risk Tree unit was 
added since the original SEPA for felling and leaving on-site trees that pose a risk to trail 
users.  

The objectives for the Douglas-fir treatments are to shift from overly dense stands to less-dense, 
more diverse and drought-resistant conifer stands; prevent density-dependent tree mortality; slow the spread of laminated root rot and plant with rot-resistant species. In the red alder stands, 
treatments will transition the forest from declining alders to more diverse, climate resilient mixed 
species stands. The treatments will generate timber revenue to support forest stewardship in line 
with the property’s working forest designation, defined in King County’s Comprehensive Plan 
(2022). 

DRNP proposes using logging equipment such as feller-bunchers, skidders, processors, log loaders, forwarders, shovel yarding, or other similar mechanized methods of tree cutting to remove Douglas-fir up to 24” diameter at breast height (DBH). Western redcedar and other root rot-resistant species would be retained. Most declining red alder over 8” DBH in E units would be removed, and all other species retained. The cut trees would be sold for lumber, chips, pulp, veneer, firewood, or other uses as markets allow. Stumps will typically remain unless pulled in root rot-infested stands to deter spread.

Description of Proposal:
King County Road Services Division (Roads) is proposing a project at the four-leg intersection of Southeast (SE) Green Valley Road and 218th Avenue Southeast. SE Green Valley Road is a rural minor collector and 218th Avenue SE is a major arterial. This intersection services the traveling public from the cities of Auburn, Black Diamond, Covington, Enumclaw, and Kent. As these cities grow in population, the volume of traffic at the intersection increases. This intersection is a high-collision location. In 2021, the intersection was upgraded to an all-way stop as an interim safety measure to reduce right-angle collisions. To further improve visibility, flashing lights were added to the stop signs in 2025. A new single-lane roundabout will be constructed to ease congestion and improve intersection safety. By reducing the frequency and severity of collisions, the project ensures a more reliable flow of traffic. Additionally, the plan includes essential drainage upgrades, featuring a permanent stormwater infiltration pond.
The estimated total project cost is $3.1 million. Project design has been funded through federal and local county funds. Roads is currently seeking additional funding for construction and right-of-way acquisition.
